question: Do we always need the most powerful AI, or is a good enough tool often the wiser choice?
reflection: Choosing the right size of tool for each task can make AI affordable for more organisations and leave more resources for people.

sources.subject: Inside the pragmatic AI engineer's new secret weapon

one_line: Teams are shifting from chasing the smartest model to mixing cheaper open models for routine work with frontier models for hard cases.

top_stories.title: Inkling as a practical open choice
top_stories.what: A deep dive argues that Thinking Machines' Inkling is not the strongest model overall but is the leading US open model and is easy to deploy from day one.
top_stories.why: For most research tasks a cheaper, controllable model may give similar results at a fraction of the cost.

top_stories.title: Fewer tokens per task
top_stories.what: Benchmark data cited in the piece suggests Inkling uses far fewer output tokens per task than rival open models, which lowers running cost.
top_stories.why: Cost per finished task, not price per token, is the right number for comparing tools in a proposal.

top_stories.title: Fine-tuning without an ML team
top_stories.what: Inkling links to Tinker, a managed service where organisations upload their own data and train a custom version without managing GPUs.
top_stories.why: This lowers the barrier for building a specialised model for one sector, such as health or labour data.

top_stories.title: Open AI research is global
top_stories.what: The article notes that Inkling borrowed architecture ideas from Chinese labs and used some data generated by Chinese models in training.
top_stories.why: Model origins are mixed, so procurement rules based only on a lab's country may be hard to apply.

saudi_lens.text: Self-hosted open models that can be fine-tuned on local data match the Kingdom's push for sovereign AI and data residency.

idea.title: Model routing review
idea.pitch: Audit which AI tasks in a project truly need a frontier model and which could move to a cheaper open model.
idea.first_step: List every AI task used in one recent project and mark each as routine or hard reasoning.

idea_kids.title: Right tool for the job
idea_kids.pitch: A sorting game where children match everyday jobs to the simplest tool that can do them, from a spoon to a power drill.
idea_kids.first_step: Print 15 picture cards of tools and 15 cards of small jobs around the house.

watchlist.name: Thinking Machines Lab
watchlist.note: Watch real enterprise use of Inkling and Tinker.

tool.name: Tinker
tool.use: Managed service for fine-tuning open models on your own data.

verify: Inkling reportedly averages about 25,000 output tokens per benchmark task, far fewer than rival open models.
Inkling's price is reportedly about $1 per million input tokens and $4 per million output tokens.

terms.definition: Sending each task to the cheapest model that can do it well, and only hard tasks to the most expensive model.
Training an existing model a little more on your own examples so it fits a specific task.
The total cost of getting one job done by an AI, including all the text it generates along the way.

concepts.summary: Cheaper open models handle most routine work at a fraction of the price.
Day-one support across platforms makes open models easy to adopt.
